entries.authors: Myroslava Hladchenko
entries.title: Foreign co-affiliations and performance measurement of universities and the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, 2020–2023
entries.primary_abstract_preview:
This study examines the role of foreign co-affiliations in shaping the research performance of Ukrainian universities and research institutes of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine (NASU) before and during Russia’s invasion. In 2023, a notable share of high-visibility articles used for institutional assessment was authored by scholars co-affiliated with both Ukrainian and foreign institutions. This share was higher for NASU (17.1%) than for universities (10.6%), reflecting NASU’s research-oriented profile and its strong focus on physical sciences & engineering. In 2022–2023, this share increased across all disciplines in both types of institutions. At universities, the strongest growth occurred in social sciences & humanities, while biomedical & health sciences lagged behind. The largest shares of articles with foreign co-affiliations involved institutions in advanced science systems such as Germany and China, as well as neighbouring Poland, Czechia, and Slovakia.

Articles with foreign co-affiliations showed citation impact comparable to internationally co-authored articles and substantially outperformed purely domestic publications.

On the one hand, articles with foreign co-affiliations ensure research continuity and enhance the citation visibility of a resource-constrained and war-affected national science system. On the other hand, they distort the measurement of the national and institutional research performance, thereby hindering reform of the national science system. Reliance solely on international links cannot substitute for a strong domestic base. Evaluation frameworks in Ukraine and other countries could be improved through a two-level differentiation, distinguishing first between types of authorship and second among types of foreign co-affiliations, taking into account their duration and the extent of co-affiliated scholars’ actual contributions.

Although this lies beyond the primary scope of the present study, the findings highlight that the institutional divide between NASU and universities in Ukraine is not justified by research performance.

entries.authors: Hou Zhu, Yihan Xiao, Wei Yan, Mengjia Wu, Yi Zhang
entries.title: Active or silent? The spiral of silence in social bots
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Despite the profound ability of social bots in influencing information dissemination, they may contrarily coincide with online users remaining silent regarding the spiral of silence theory. Therefore, it is essential to explore how social bots are associated with user engagement—specifically, whether their presence corresponds with more active or more restrained user behavior, and which characteristics of bots relate to these patterns. This study collects 35,575 blog posts from Weibo and their 81,586 associated comments about Typhoon Doksuri in 2023 and investigates the association between social bot participation and user engagement through a set of methods, including social bot detection, BERTopic model, sentiment analysis, regression analysis, etc. The findings indicate that threads with higher user engagement tend to have a greater presence of social bots, but silence could still be associated with factors, such as a high level of bot proportion, greater bot–user textual and sentiment similarity, and so on. This study will support governments, enterprises, and social media users in better understanding the mechanism of social bots in information dissemination, with enhanced capabilities in public policy and administration for public awareness, disaster control, public health, and broad social media topics.

entries.authors: Yi Zhao, Heng Zhang, Yuzhuo Wang, Ziyi Xie, Yongjun Zhu
entries.title: Influence of various novelty types on delayed scientific recognition: Insights from citation classics essays
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The diffusion of novel ideas in science is frequently constrained by established actors, resulting in delayed recognition of innovative work. However, it remains unclear whether the theoretical, methodological, and results-based novelty of scientific articles, as retrospectively reported by authors, distinctly influences recognition delays and how the compositional characteristics of author teams moderate these effects. Accordingly, this study examines the correlation between different types of ex post commentary-based scientific novelty and recognition delays, while assessing how team size and the average academic age of team members moderate these relationships. Using 2565 Citation Classics articles and their corresponding commentaries, we identify ex post novelty types from author commentaries with large language models and quantify recognition delay through awakening time. The results indicate that theoretical and methodological novelty are associated with longer recognition delays, particularly the theoretical type, whereas results-based novelty is associated with earlier recognition. Importantly, the positive effect of methodological novelty appears to depend on the specific delayed-recognition metric used. Larger teams and those with higher average academic age are associated with expedited recognition, specifically for theoretical and results-based novelty. Subsequent analyses reveal that theoretical novelty typically extends recognition for papers situated at the upper end of the awakening-time distribution, methodological novelty exhibits latency at both ends of the distribution, and results-based novelty consistently accelerates recognition. These findings enhance our understanding of how retrospectively narrated scientific novelty relates to varied recognition among eventually highly cited papers.

entries.authors: Farhan Kamrul Khan, Hazem Ibrahim, Nouar AlDahoul, Talal Rahwan, Yasir Zaki
entries.title: Who gets seen in the age of AI? Adoption patterns of large language models in scholarly writing and citation outcomes
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The rapid diffusion of generative AI tools is reshaping how scholars produce and communicate knowledge, raising questions about who benefits and who is left behind. We analyze over 230,000 Scopus-indexed computer science articles (2021–2025) to describe how stylistic markers of AI-likeness in scholarly writing co-evolve with scholarly visibility across regions. Using a zero-shot detector (Binoculars) as a proxy for AI-likeness, we document stylistic changes in writing and examine their associations with citation counts, journal placement, and global citation flows in the periods before and after the public release of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. We emphasize that the Binoculars score captures stylistic similarity to large-language-model outputs rather than confirmed AI usage, and that all reported relationships are associational rather than causal. We document several patterns: stylistic AI-likeness rises across regions after late 2022 (in the detector score, in its binary classification, and in a detector-independent lexical marker index), with a more pronounced shift among authors in the Global East; AI-like writing is associated with higher citation counts conditional on venue and journal-prominence characteristics, an association that persists when generative-AI-topic papers are controlled for or excluded and replicates under a second neural detector, though it attenuates under the coarser lexical measure; more human-like writing is conversely associated with placement in higher-tier journals; and global citation networks show a modest eastward tilt in visibility alongside tighter intra-regional clustering, with country-level changes in AI-likeness unrelated to changes in network position. These patterns are consistent with a co-occurring reconfiguration of scholarly writing and recognition around the diffusion of generative AI, but we cannot rule out concurrent topic shifts, productivity effects, and the broader rise of generative-AI research within computer science as alternative explanations.

entries.authors: Yaniasih Yaniasih, Ambar Yoganingrum, Aria Bisri, Ekawati Marlina, ... Rulina Rachmawati
entries.title: Understanding self-citation: A statistical and contextual analysis of bibliographic and in-text citation in Indonesian social sciences
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Self-citation remains a contested practice in bibliometrics and is often treated as a uniform indicator, despite important distinctions between its in-text and bibliographic forms. This study examines patterns and meanings of self-citation among Indonesian social science researchers by combining quantitative statistical analysis with qualitative contextual analysis of in-text citations. A total of 3735 references from 537 Scopus-indexed articles authored by researchers affiliated with the National Research and Innovation Agency were analyzed using a custom-built citation parsing system. The system integrates four analytical dimensions (location, sentiment, function, and source role) to capture the contextual meanings of self-citation. Findings show that in-text self-citations predominantly occur in the Introduction section, mainly serving explanatory functions with largely neutral sentiment and frequently referencing prior Results sections. Statistical analysis identified significant differences between in-text and bibliographic self-citations, suggesting that in-text citation patterns may reflect contextual dimensions not captured by conventional citation counts alone. Differences in self-citation frequency were also observed across collaboration types and authorship patterns. These findings highlight the value of incorporating citation-context analysis to complement traditional bibliometric approaches and provide a more context-sensitive understanding of self-citation practices in scholarly communication.

entries.authors: Kuei-Kuei Lai, Yu-Jin Hsu, Chih-Wen Hsiao
entries.title: Revealing patterns of strategic knowledge evolution with BERTopic: Semantic–temporal trajectories via transparent adjacent-year linking in strategic management
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Strategic management research is theoretically plural and continuously reconfigures through the appearance, persistence, branching, and merging of ideas. Yet most large-scale mappings rely on citations or bag-of-words topic models, offering limited support for tracking semantic drift and summarizing cross-temporal change as reproducible, event-like patterns. We address this gap with an unsupervised semantic-temporal pipeline that couples BERTopic with adjacent-year Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) matrices, which are used strictly as a transparent linkage rule. Using a PRISMA-screened Web of Science query (search window 1980–2025), we analyze 25,907 English-language journal articles spanning 1984–2025. BERTopic produces 222 fine-grained topics for temporal-network construction; a coherence-screened subset of 33 topics (topic coherence score above 0.8) is used separately for high-confidence Fish-Scale theory mapping. Yearly centroids of the 222 topics are linked across adjacent years, and five descriptive event signatures–Inheritance, Differentiation, Convergence, Emergence, and Extinction-are classified using explicit threshold and configuration criteria. The 222-topic trajectories reveal four eras (IO/Porter → RBV → KBV-DCV → Digital/Ecosystem) and a long-run shift from early topic-population churn toward stronger branching and recombination. This dual-resolution design preserves structural coverage for evolutionary analysis while reserving the most coherent topics for disciplinary interpretation.

entries.authors: Lutz Bornmann
entries.title: To sign or not to sign initiatives to reform research evaluation: A discussion of the pros and cons
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The integration of bibliometrics into science governance has fundamentally transformed scientific practices, leading to unintended consequences such as goal displacement and citizen bibliometrics. In response, international reform movements like the Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment (CoARA) advocate for responsible research assessment and the primacy of qualitative peer review. This short communication examines the commonalities and differences of these movements and weighs the pros and cons for research organizations considering signing them. While endorsement offers socio-political legitimacy and can catalyze internal modernization toward improved evaluation processes, organizations are also confronted with certain challenges. These include the potential neglect of disciplinary evaluation cultures, the high administrative burden of qualitative review, and the prevalent risk of purely symbolic uptake. Acknowledging the limitations of current empirical evidence, this commentary concludes that the future of research assessment relies not on universal declarations, but on the development of process-specific evaluation designs. Strategic principles for implementation – such as tailoring assessments to specific occasions, respecting epistemic diversity, safeguarding data sovereignty, empowering evaluation committees, evaluating assessment procedures, and professionalizing evaluative bibliometrics – are proposed to advance responsible evaluative practices.

entries.authors: Zhu Liang, Shengzhi Huang, Leyan Wu, Qikai Cheng, Wei Lu
entries.title: Presentation styles in academic videos: Unveiling their relationships with scholarly impact and research novelty
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Academic videos (AcVs) have emerged as a critical medium in multi-modal scholarly communication. Authors’ presentation styles in AcVs, operationalized as multimodal design strategies through temporal allocation, spatial distribution, and presentation speed across modality types and functional structures, provide valuable insights into how scientific knowledge is communicated and disseminated. However, existing studies have primarily focused on static, text-based communication, leaving multi-modal videos largely unexplored. To address this gap, we develop a dedicated analytical framework that applies AI techniques to understand and analyze AcVs. Furthermore, we introduce novel metrics to characterize presentation styles across temporal, visual, and speed dimensions. We also measure scholarly impact using citation-based indicators and assess research novelty using both embedding-based similarity and large language model (LLM) evaluations. Drawing on a dataset comprising 438 papers from ACL 2021 and their corresponding videos, we conduct a systematic analysis of authors’ presentation styles and examine their associations with both scholarly impact and perceived novelty. The results indicate that AcVs prioritize methodological and empirical sections through longer, multi-modally coordinated presentation. Our regression analyses further reveal that structured and balanced delivery is positively associated with higher impact, while visually rich and well-paced presentations, particularly in the method and experiment & conclusion sections, are linked to greater research novelty. This study represents the first attempt to quantitatively analyze presentation styles in AcVs and examine their associations with scholarly impact and novelty.

entries.title: Contextual patterns of journal self-citation in JCR-suppressed and comparator journals: a multi-dimensional citation content analysis

entries.authors: Songlin Cai, Xianwen Wang
entries.title: Score increases, author–reviewer communication, and subsequent citations in open peer review: Evidence from ICLR
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Communication between authors and reviewers in peer review is widely viewed as contributing to manuscript improvement. Further analyses show that score increases are associated with more intensive exchanges; DeBERTa-v3 classification of the messages also links score increases to academic, evaluative, and procedural communication. These findings document conditional associations between score trajectories, communication patterns, and subsequent scholarly uptake in forum-based OPR.

entries.primary_abstract_preview: It has been argued that concentrating research resources is necessary to maintain Sweden’s competitiveness as a research nation. These findings challenge prevailing assumptions and support a more equitable allocation of research funding, contributing to a broader and more sustainable research ecosystem in Sweden.

entries.title: Specialization indicators in scientometrics: Understanding the Activity Index and the F-measure through their underlying components
entries.primary_abstract_preview: This study provides a conceptual and analytical clarification of the Activity Index (AI) and the F-measure by identifying the structural relationships with their underlying share components and explaining their context-dependent properties. entries.title: Rethinking thematic evolution in science mapping:An integrated framework for longitudinal analysis
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Strategic diagrams and co-word analysis are widely employed to examine the conceptual structure of scientific domains and their development over time. This study introduces a structurally integrated framework in which lineage reconstruction is embedded within the same weighted relational architecture that underpins cross-sectional detection. The approach models thematic continuity through graded document affiliation and a lineage-strength measure integrating directional thematic coverage and centrality-weighted structural coherence, thereby reconceptualising evolution as the reconfiguration of relational structures rather than the persistence of surface vocabulary. It also reduces hub-centred artefacts arising from purely lexical lineage reconstruction. By aligning thematic detection and temporal modelling within a unified relational paradigm, the framework enhances the methodological coherence and interpretive robustness of longitudinal science mapping.

entries.title: A revised disruption index considering detailed citation information: Enhancing noise resistance and differentiation
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The disruption index (DI), proposed to reflect the extent of scientific breakthroughs brought about by a patent or paper, was defined based on citation relationships. entries.authors: Juan Gorraiz
entries.title: “What cannot be said cannot be measured”: On the philosophical foundations and limits of bibliometrics
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Bibliometric indicators play a central role in contemporary research evaluation, shaping decisions about funding, careers, and institutional legitimacy. While extensive critical work has examined their methodological limitations and practical effects, less attention has been paid to the philosophical assumptions—and conceptual limits—that render bibliometric evaluation intelligible and authoritative in the first place. This article addresses that gap by analysing the foundations of bibliometrics through a series of interconnected philosophical problem-spaces. The article examines bibliometric evaluation as a regime of knowledge that rests on specific ontological, epistemological, temporal, and normative assumptions. Ontologically, bibliometrics presupposes a conception of scholarly activity as a collection of discrete and stabilised outputs rather than as a processual practice. Epistemologically, it equates measurability with visibility, thereby privileging what can be rendered comparable over what can be meaningfully understood. Temporally, it favours short-term recognition and cumulative continuity, making it poorly equipped to capture conceptual rupture, delayed impact, and paradigm change. Drawing on a range of philosophical perspectives—including Kant, Wittgenstein, Kuhn, Marx, Foucault, Bourdieu, and Feyerabend—the article shows how bibliometric indicators function not merely as descriptive tools, but as instruments of valuation, normalisation, and power. Particular attention is paid to contemporary developments such as Open Access, new metrics, and normative frameworks within scientometrics, which are interpreted as sites of paradigmatic tension rather than straightforward solutions to the limits of evaluation. The article argues that the constraints of bibliometric evaluation are not accidental or merely technical, but structural and conceptual. Rather than calling for ever more refined indicators, it advocates a reflexive and pluralistic understanding of evaluation that recognises the contingency of metrics, remains attentive to what resists quantification, and resists the naturalisation of particular evaluative regimes. In doing so, the article contributes to a philosophical rethinking of bibliometrics as a practice that both reveals and reshapes—and necessarily leaves unsaid—key dimensions of scholarly knowledge.

entries.title: A novel indicator h* to measure research efficiency and identify researchers facing challenges: Application to engineering sciences
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The classical h index is a widely used metric to evaluate a researcher’s scientific impact by combining productivity and citation counts. However, its main limitation lies in its cumulative nature. Indeed, the h index never decreases, which can mask recent changes in research activity or productivity, especially in late career stages, post retirement or when researchers stop publishing and contributing to scientific work due to administrative responsibilities, a focus on teaching, exclusion from research teams or a deliberate career transition away from research. This can lead to biased comparisons between junior and senior researchers, failing to reflect current research dynamics. To address these issues, this paper proposes a new metric, the h* index, which extends the classical h index by incorporating temporal elements of a researcher career. The h* index considers active publication periods and citation rates relative to career length, making it a dynamic and updatable indicator. This allows for early detection of declining productivity, thematic isolation or shifts toward non research duties, providing a more nuanced and fair assessment of scientific performance. Moreover, given that some countries, including France, hesitate to rely solely on traditional bibliometric indices, the h* index offers a complementary tool designed for continuous career monitoring. By combining robustness and adaptability, this new metric aims to better support research evaluation and management decisions in academic institutions.

entries.authors: Liwei Zhang, Jue Wang
entries.title: Is equal credit really equal? The impact of academic evaluation policies on authorship decisions
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Performance-based evaluation policies can unintentionally reshape research behavior, especially when academic recognition is tied to narrow authorship metrics. This study examines how such policies influence equal contribution authorship (ECA) in Chinese universities and research institutions, focusing on Cell Biology, where multi-authored publications are common. Using a dataset of 30,708 articles published in leading Cell Biology journals between 2001 and 2024, we employ two complementary difference-in-differences strategies. First, using domestically authored publications, we show that after the introduction of performance-based evaluation policies around 2008, Chinese-authored articles experienced significant increases in the number of lead, first, and corresponding authors relative to other countries. Second, using the full sample, we apply a categorical exposure-based design and find that these effects are concentrated in papers with substantial Chinese author participation. Across both specifications, no comparable effect is observed for non-lead authors. The findings suggest that evaluation policies primarily reallocate authorship recognition within papers rather than expanding team size, with implications for more balanced research assessment systems.

entries.authors: Saeyoung Choi, Junghye Lee
entries.title: Revealing country-level disparities in researchers’ transition to artificial intelligence: A two-stage analytical framework
entries.primary_abstract_preview: As artificial intelligence (AI) has become a general tool for scientific research, researchers’ transition to AI from diverse disciplinary backgrounds reflects the adaptability of national research systems to this transformative technological change. Descriptive comparisons of country-level transition rates can be misleading, as they may reflect differences in the composition of individual researchers rather than systematic contextual influences. This study proposes a two-stage analytical framework to estimate country-level disparities in researchers’ transition to AI under high-dimensional individual heterogeneity. In the first stage, a deep learning model based on publication sequences and collaboration networks estimates each researcher’s transition propensity, capturing the expected likelihood of transition given each researcher’s profile. In the second stage, these estimates are used in a country fixed-effects regression model to estimate residual cross-country disparities among researchers with comparable profiles. Analyzing 1,599,440 researchers across 18 countries, we find substantial disparities in transition to AI that remain after adjustment, with South Korea and Russia at the positive and negative extremes, respectively. The overall pattern is robust across alternative adjustment models but heterogeneous across disciplines. These findings indicate that cross-country differences in transition to AI persist beyond research trajectories or collaboration networks. We provide a composition-adjusted basis for comparing national research systems, informing science policy strategies.

entries.authors: Alex J. Yang, Yujie Shi, Fanming Wang, Xinyu Song, Sanhong Deng
entries.title: Distant but bridgeable: how geographic and cognitive distance jointly shape interdisciplinary knowledge production
entries.primary_abstract_preview: We introduce a distance mismatch perspective and examine how geographic and cognitive distance jointly influence interdisciplinarity. Using a large-scale dataset of over 31 million team-authored publications from the OpenAlex database, we measure interdisciplinarity using the Rao–Stirling index based on the disciplinary composition of references. Team cognitive distance is constructed from time-aware author embeddings derived from SPECTER2, while geographic distance is measured using institutional affiliation coordinates. We find that both geographic and cognitive distance are positively associated with interdisciplinarity when considered independently. However, their joint effect reveals a more nuanced pattern. Geographic distance enhances interdisciplinarity only when teams are cognitively diverse. When cognitive distance is low, geographically local teams perform equally well or better. Decomposing interdisciplinarity into variety, balance, and disparity further shows that geographic distance amplifies the breadth and cognitive reach of knowledge integration, but at the cost of reduced balance. These findings demonstrate that the benefits of geographic dispersion are conditional on cognitive structure, highlighting the importance of aligning spatial and intellectual dimensions in scientific collaboration.

entries.authors: Bingyi Wu, Tianjun Wu, Yanmeng Xing, Xinzhi Xie, Chao Min
entries.title: The role of interdisciplinary funding in supporting impactful interdisciplinary research
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Funding interdisciplinary research (IDR) has long been contested. Funders rely on interdisciplinary projects (IDPs) to address complex problems, yet IDPs often face lower funding success and are perceived as riskier. Empirical understanding of how interdisciplinary funding shapes IDR remains limited, leaving it unclear whether interdisciplinary funding designs effectively improve the impact of IDR. We investigate this issue using a unique dataset covering 604,618 projects funded by the world's three largest public funders—NSF, NSFC, and NIH—between 1965 and 2024, and 3,892,779 publications supported by these projects. We train a deep learning model on the scientific text of more than one million publications to capture the semantic signatures of disciplinary knowledge, and use it to identify IDPs, showing that it can reliably infer the disciplinary distribution of funded projects and predict the interdisciplinarity of resulting publications. Our results indicate that, on average, the interdisciplinarity of funded papers is negatively associated with their citation performance. However, it translates into citation gains only when a paper is supported through an IDP—especially IDPs that recombine atypical and more distant disciplines. These associations remain robust after partly addressing selection effects; a funded-versus-unfunded comparison further points to a distinct IDP—but not monodisciplinary projects—funding effect. Overall, our findings suggest that IDP funding is closely associated with the scientific impact of IDR, and that funders may be able to use interdisciplinary funding designs to support high-impact IDR. Meanwhile, our findings also highlight that both funders and researchers should attend to the alignment between a project's interdisciplinary strategy and its research practice when making funding and application decisions.

entries.authors: Karolina Tchilinguirova, Khadija Aftab, Amanuel Aknaw, Alvine Boaye Belle, Oluwafemi Odu
entries.title: CiteFairly: Toward the improvement of gendered citation practices in the software engineering field
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Several studies have established that citation biases are pervasive in several STEM disciplines (e.g., Neuroscience, Physics, Computer Science). Indeed, scientific articles written by authors belonging to certain socio-cultural groups (e.g., women, Hispanics, Black) are usually significantly less cited than articles written by authors belonging to dominant groups. This trend is more exacerbated in the software engineering (SE) field where articles written by researchers from some socio-cultural groups (e.g., women) are considerably under-cited. Since the number of citations plays a key role in scientific circles, unfairness in citation practices therefore has an adverse impact on the recruitment, salaries, retention, promotion, and recognition of some researchers. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to improve citation diversity in the reference lists of manuscripts that will be submitted for publication in software engineering venues. Thus, for each manuscript under analysis, our approach first identifies potential citation biases in its reference list, then attempts to mitigate these biases by recommending to its authors relevant articles written by other authors from diverse backgrounds. We implemented our approach as an online tool called CiteFairly. The latter is built atop several bibliometric tools such as: OpenAlex, Gender-API, and Semantic Scholar. To validate our approach, we conducted various experiments on the reference lists of papers published in several editions of well-established Software Engineering conferences. Our experimental results show that our approach can accurately identify and mitigate gendered citation biases in the analyzed reference lists with automated gender distributions deviating from manual annotations by no more than 5 percentage points on average.

entries.authors: F. Pacheco-Torgal
entries.title: The illusion of scientific talent identification through publication counts: a critical commentary on Haunschild and Bornmann
entries.primary_abstract_preview: This letter responds to the article by Haunschild and Bornmann, published in the Journal of Informetrics, which proposes a bibliometric framework for identifying promising early-career scientists based on three specific indicators: the number of publications in top-quartile journals (Q1), total publication output (O), and corresponding authorship (C). Using the combined OxQ1 indicator, the authors compile a dataset of 46,200 individuals classified as “potentially talented,” intended to support informed peer review and hiring decisions. This commentary directly examines the methodological assumptions underlying the authors’ indicator selection and their validation strategy. The use of Q1—a journal-level quartile metric—as a proxy for individual research quality is problematic, particularly given the authors’ own acknowledgment of the Journal Impact Factor’s limitations. More critically, the authors’ own validation analysis yields type I and type II error rates of approximately 28–30%, raising serious questions about the OxQ1 combination’s reliability for the talent identification purposes proposed. The reliance on total publication output (O) as a core indicator risks conflating productivity with intellectual contribution, while the public release of a dataset labeling 46,200 researchers as “potentially talented” carries methodological and ethical implications that this letter addresses directly. The argument is not that bibliometrics lacks value, nor that Q1 journals lack quality, but that talent is a capacity which cannot be read off counts of output and journal placement; the letter explains why and points to indicators better suited to assessing individuals.

entries.authors: Si Shen, Chuan Jiang, Dongbo Wang, Zhixiao Zhao, ... Jia Tina Du
entries.title: A novel knowledge-entity-grounded scholarly retrieval framework in full-text academic documents
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Entity-centric retrieval in full-text scholarly documents remains underdeveloped, despite the growing need for fine-grained access to knowledge embedded within them. Query-relevant knowledge is often concentrated in a limited number of sentences rather than distributed evenly across an entire document. To address this gap, this study develops a Knowledge-Entity-Grounded Scholarly Retrieval Framework comprising Knowledge-Entity-Bearing Evidence Identification and Structure-Guided Relevance Ranking. The framework is evaluated on a primary corpus of 5356 full-text articles from JASIST, IPM, LISR, and ASIST proceedings published between 2010 and 2023. The corpus was manually annotated for knowledge entities and rhetorical structure. SciBERT achieves the best performance for evidence identification (F1 = 94.17%), and the knowledge-entity-aware ALBERT-Ranking model improves NDCG@1 and NDCG@10 by 12.54 and 6.38 percentage points over BM25. External validation on 957 Journal of Informetrics articles published between 2010 and 2020 confirms that the framework transfers effectively to unseen literature. The results indicate that grounding relevance ranking in knowledge-entity-bearing evidence and rhetorical structure can improve full-text scholarly retrieval.

entries.authors: Jeongyeon Choi, Yi Zhao, Yongjun Zhu
entries.title: Does the Matthew effect exist in open peer review? An empirical study of institutional prestige effects on review outcomes
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The phenomenon of cumulative advantage, known as the Matthew Effect, has been extensively observed in the scientific community. However, less is known about how cumulative advantage manifests through institutional prestige during the evaluative phase of open peer review (OPR). In this study, we investigate whether authors’ institutional prestige influences review outcomes in OPR and, if so, the extent of that influence. Examining all research and review articles published on the open-access publishing platform F1000Research from 2012 to 2025, we assess the effects of institutional prestige on OPR review outcomes using coarsened exact matching (CEM). To isolate the effect of institutional prestige from other determinants of review outcomes, we controlled for authors’ scholarly impact using the h-index and article-level differences using measures of novelty and readability. The results indicate that (1) institutional prestige is positively associated with peer review evaluations, (2) its effects vary across review criteria, (3) it leads to shorter review periods, and (4) its effects weaken as authors accumulate greater scholarly impact. This study advances the scholarly understanding of the Matthew Effect in OPR and devises recommendations for reviewers, editors, and policymakers.

entries.authors: Mu-hsuan Huang, Yuntong Xiao, Xiaojuan Liu
entries.title: Exploring the impact of super-cited papers on counting methods, counting inflation and university rankings: Evidence from engineering
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The distribution of citation counts across publications is highly skewed, with a small subset of super-cited papers, defined in this study as those ranking in the top 0.1% by cumulative citations, receiving disproportionately high citation counts. Using universities in the engineering field and its subfield, environmental engineering, from the NTU Rankings (2014 to 2023) as the analytical sample, this study applies four counting methods to examine how super-cited papers influence university rankings. The results indicate that high-ranking universities generally experience counting inflation but maintain relatively stable positions, whereas lower-ranking universities are more sensitive to the inclusion of a few super-cited papers. Although inflation occurs less frequently among these institutions, its magnitude is often substantial when it does arise. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the environmental engineering subfield, which exhibits a higher proportion and broader distribution of super-cited papers. Despite these differences, rankings obtained through the four counting methods remain highly correlated, with harmonic counting and straight-first-author counting showing the highest consistency because both emphasize first-author contributions. At the national level, Chinese universities show the most pronounced ranking changes, with their positions improving after the exclusion of super-cited papers, whereas universities in the United States and the United Kingdom display relatively modest variations. Within the environmental engineering subfield, rankings are more strongly affected and display higher sensitivity to these papers than in the broader field. These findings underscore the importance of considering ranking intervals, disciplinary level, counting method, and national context when interpreting university rankings in research evaluation.

entries.authors: Ying Lou, Zhengyi Zhou, Guosheng Wang, Zhesi Shen, Menghui Li
entries.title: The landscape of problematic papers in the field of non-coding RNA
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Retractions have increased sharply in recent years, alongside a growing number of papers that receive post-publication comments questioning their reliability (commented papers). Together, retracted and commented papers undermine the credibility of scientific research and may also threaten public health. In this study, we examine problematic papers in the field of non-coding RNA (ncRNA) from multiple perspectives to identify common patterns and inform strategies for addressing large-scale fraudulent publications. We find that studies on under-investigated ncRNAs are more likely to become problematic papers. These papers often show substantial textual similarity, and many additional papers with similar text also display suspicious image duplication. Healthcare institutions, particularly those with lower publication output, appear especially vulnerable to producing such papers. Most problematic papers are concentrated in a small set of journals, many of which do not adequately address concerns raised after publication. Overall, our findings indicate that a substantial number of problematic papers may remain undetected and that their shared characteristics can support more effective strategies for identifying and curbing large-scale fraudulent publications.

entries.title: The Price–Pareto growth model of networks with community structure
entries.primary_abstract_preview: We introduce a new analytical framework for modelling degree sequences in individual communities of real-world networks, e.g., citations to papers in different fields. Our work is inspired by a recent modification of the Price’s model, which assumes that citations are gained partly accidentally, and to some extent preferentially. Our work addresses the need to represent the heterogeneity of various scientific domains, as standard homogeneous models fail to capture the distinct growth ratios and citing cultures of different fields. Extending the model to networks with a community structure allows us to devise the analytical formulae for, amongst others, citation counts in each cluster and their inequality as described by the Gini index. We also show that a citation count distribution in each community tends to a Pareto type II distribution. Thanks to the derived model parameter estimators, the new model can be fitted to real citation and similar networks.

entries.authors: Sadaf Sultana, Sajid Ali, Ismail Shah
entries.title: Modeling zero-inflated and heavy-tailed citation data using Bayesian hurdle quantile regression with flexible distributions
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Citation data are often characterized by excess zeros, strong skewness, and heavy tails, making them challenging to model with standard regression techniques. Traditional Bayesian quantile regression based on the asymmetric Laplace distribution (ALD) is commonly used but struggles to accommodate these complexities. This study introduces a Bayesian hurdle quantile regression (BHQR) model that adopts a two-part framework: a hurdle component to handle excess zeros and low citation counts, and a quantile regression component to model positive outcomes. To overcome the limitations of the ALD, the model employs more flexible distributions, including log-logistic, Weibull, and generalized exponential. Parameters are estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, supported by extensive simulation studies across various quantiles and sample sizes. Model performance is assessed through mean squared error, mean absolute error, pinball loss function, prediction error, and credible interval width. The results demonstrate that hurdle-based models with flexible distributions consistently outperform standard Bayesian quantile regression in managing zero-inflation. Application to real citation data further highlights the model’s ability to distinguish between low- and highly-cited articles, providing deeper insights into research impact. Overall, the BHQR framework offers an accurate and adaptable approach for citation analysis and can be extended to other forms of zero-inflated or heavy-tailed data in the social sciences.

entries.authors: Alejandro Espinosa-Rada
entries.title: Network positions within scholars and intellectual networks
entries.primary_abstract_preview:
Understanding the structural predominance of researchers within scientific specialties requires moving beyond conventional bibliometric indicators such as citation counts or h-indices. We propose a multidimensional dominance framework based on hyper-events — ordered quadruples linking an author of a citing paper to an author of the paper it cites — capturing the full relational chain: author  →  citing paper  →  cited paper  →  author. Using a bounded bibliographic dataset of Chilean astronomers and astrophysicists, we operationalize a Pareto-style neighborhood inclusion criterion to identify authors whose relational neighborhoods encompass those of others across multiple mechanisms: productive capacity, citation reach, and recognition.

Our analysis reveals a layered structure of dominance, where maximal authors occupy relational positions not enclosed by any other researcher. We demonstrate that multiple incomparable maximal authors coexist, reflecting structural pluralism within the field. The framework highlights the importance of relational breadth over simple intensity measures, showing that dominance arises from strategically positioned publications and citations rather than sheer output volume or first authorship.

These results suggest that scientific predominance is best conceptualized as a positional phenomenon within relational networks. The hyper-event approach preserves multidimensionality, captures local hierarchies, and provides a robust alternative to scalar metrics, offering new insights into the organization and stratification of scientific specialties.

entries.authors: Shan Huang, Jin Mao, Kun Lu, Gang Li
entries.title: Originated versus imported knowledge: Revisiting the relationship between novelty and academic impact
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Knowledge innovation is considered one key driver of scientific impact. However, current studies overlook how cross-field knowledge flows shape novel knowledge creation, and our understanding of its creation patterns and relationship to scientific impact remains incomplete. By introducing a broader scientific context of over 30 million biomedical publications, this study uses biomedical entities and entity combinations identified through automated recognition as proxies for knowledge and quantifies paper impact by citation counts, using Alzheimer’s disease as an empirical case. We classify novel knowledge into either originated or imported based on whether the original source is the focal field, and subsequently analyze its distribution patterns and relationships with impact. The results show that 85.82% of novel entities and 55.84% of novel combinations are imported, indicating the dominance of imported knowledge. Regardless of knowledge sources, higher novel entity proportions are associated with reduced paper impact, and novel combination proportions show an inverted U-shaped relationship with impact, but the source affects relationship intensities. It is also evidenced that originated knowledge is more strongly associated with internal impact, while imported knowledge is more strongly associated with external impact. entries.authors: Wen Lou, Tan Fu, Mingzhu Gao, Qianqian Xu
entries.title: The diffusion of artificial intelligence methods in scientific research: growth pattern, disciplinary variation, and task alignment
entries.primary_abstract_preview: How AI methods are integrated into scientific research remains poorly understood despite the rapid growth of AI adoption in science. This study provides large-scale empirical documentation of this integration, analyzing 27,636,491 Web of Science publications from 2000 to 2022. Using a task-oriented AI method classification system from Papers with Code, a three-round LLM-based identification pipeline, bibliometric analysis, co-occurrence network analysis, and an entropy-weighted TOPSIS evaluation framework, we identify 361,480 AI application papers spanning 867 distinct methods. Three principal patterns emerge. First, the share of publications employing AI methods almost tripled between 2018 and 2022, with AI present in at least 120 WoS subfields by the end of the period. Second, adoption rates vary by more than an order of magnitude across disciplines (from approximately 9% in Engineering sciences to below 1.5% in the Humanities sciences), a pattern consistent with differences in disciplinary knowledge forms. These findings characterize AI integration as a process of functional stratification, and suggest the pre-2022 methodological ecosystem formed a critical foundation for the emergence of generative AI in science.

entries.primary_abstract_preview: The assessments of national involvement in the global system for exchange of knowledge traditionally focus on each country’s active contribution in the form of scientific publications and their citation impact. entries.title: Textual content and academic journals selectivity: A case of economic journals
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Currently, a significant influx of submissions poses challenges to the editorial processes of scientific journals, particularly top-tier academic periodicals. Finally, prompt-based zero-shot classification with proprietary large language models yields heterogeneous accuracy and does not outperform fine-tuned SciBERT. Although our model relies solely on linguistic features, it may assist editors in the initial screening of submissions, but does not assess scientific novelty or intrinsic scholarly quality.

entries.authors: Xingpeng Liu, An Zeng, Xiaohua Cui
entries.title: Breaking through the constraints of academic social capital: Insights from top scientists’ collaboration strategies
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Academic social capital, owing to its potential to be converted into a variety of explicit and tacit resources, is of profound strategic significance throughout the academic trajectories of researchers. Employing second-order ego-network approach, we examine social capital-based collaboration strategies across three elite groups (top 1‰publications, top 1‰citations, and major award recipients) within the APS dataset comprising 227,107 scientists (1893–2009). Our research reveals that highly productive scientists employ a resource absorption strategy, by engaging in high-intensity scientific cooperation with their partners in relatively small team sizes, they efficiently connect and absorb the surrounding social capital, ultimately occupying the absolute core position in their collaborative networks. In contrast, highly cited scientists utilize a social resource dependency strategy, they seek endorsement and empowerment by attaching themselves to the periphery of collaboration networks of authoritative collaborators and larger research teams. Highly innovative scientists adopt a resource integration strategy, preferring to lead their research collaborations through the anti-preferential attachment approach with small team sizes. Devoid of substantial academic social capital advantages, they efficiently bridge academic resources across different research communities as weakly-tied “outsiders”, ultimately occupying structural holes of their collaboration networks. Our findings provide valuable insights for early-career scientists to formulate long-term development strategies and short-term collaborative tactics for their scientific careers.

entries.title: Coordination complexity and its impact on disruption: A functional lead perspective
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Research collaboration has become the dominant mode of knowledge production, yet the "coordination complexity " inherent in teamwork remain an under-explored constraint on disruption. Specifically, SS, AAG, and GD are all significantly and negatively associated with research disruption. These findings provide actionable insights for the Science of Team Science (SciTS), guiding funding agencies, institutions, and researchers in structuring collaborations for maximum research disruption.

entries.primary_abstract_preview: Our work elaborates on the study of how the choice of databases affects the measurement of scientific impact. entries.title: Modeling the impact of research data unavailability on science
entries.primary_abstract_preview:

These findings provide quantitative evidence of the systemic consequences of data unavailability and underline the importance of long-term data preservation and accessibility policies in scientific research.

entries.title: Auditable bibliometric analysis: a generic data pipeline for research evaluation
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Bibliometric analyses are widely used in research evaluation, but workflows built on dynamic citation databases can be difficult to audit and rerun because database contents evolve and key procedural decisions are often under-documented. This study identifies where auditability breaks down in Scopus-based workflows and specifies a generic, tool-agnostic bibliometric pipeline, where “generic” refers to transferable workflow logic and provenance artefacts rather than database-independent access or metadata conditions. We used three large-scale case studies as diagnostic material, reconstructing their workflows, benchmarking them against published reproducibility guidance, and conducting a structured failure mode analysis from query specification and data acquisition to cleaning, enrichment, analysis, and reporting. The results show that core descriptive elements are usually reported, but crucial provenance details for audit and reruns are often missing, especially retrieval route, export and batching logic, merge decisions, snapshot timing, and analysis parameters. In response, we specify an artefact-based six-stage pipeline that operationalises documentation by default through preserved queries, manifests, logs, rules, and parameter records, thereby strengthening auditability and structured rerun capability in dynamic database settings.

entries.authors: Elena Álvarez-García, Daniel García-Costa, Flaminio Squazzoni, Mario Malički, ... Francisco Grimaldo
entries.title: Published peer review reports have higher informative content than unpublished reports
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Although publishing peer review reports increases editorial transparency, little is known about the differences in terms of information content, readability and similarity between open and unpublished peer review reports across journals. We compared 140,844 published and 117,250 unpublished peer review reports from 233 medical journals published by Elsevier and Springer Nature between 2016 and 2021 using natural language processing. Our results showed that published peer review reports were longer and had more informative content, with the greatest difference found in the number of “suggestion and solution” sentences. Published peer review reports were also more readable and more similar to each other in terms of content structure. Reports by women had higher information scores and were more readable than reports by men, while reports by reviewers from non-Western institutions had lower information scores and were less readable than reports by reviewers from Western institutions. Our results suggest that increasing the transparency of review reports could lead to more detailed reports focusing on suggestions for improving manuscripts.

entries.authors: Weiye Gu, Chaoqun Ni
entries.title: Universities as central actors in evidence-based policymaking in the US
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Understanding how universities contribute to policymaking is crucial for assessing the societal impact of research. This study analyzes 80,650 U.S. policy documents (2017–2022) that cite 295,428 US-affiliated academic publications, linking Overton policy data with Scopus affiliation records and federal research funding from the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. Universities account for over 70 % of all policy-cited research, confirming their central role in evidence-informed governance. Yet this influence is uneven: a small number of research-intensive institutions dominate, while most universities contribute modestly. Health sciences account for the largest share of university-cited research, with additional contributions in economics, education, and social sciences. Federal agencies cite university research more heavily than local governments or think tanks, and policy visibility is geographically concentrated in states with strong research ecosystems. Correlation analyses indicate that productivity, federal funding, and institutional prestige strongly predict policy influence, whereas government involvement is not consistently associated.

entries.authors: Yunhao You, Nian Liu, Qian Yu
entries.title: Weak ties in scientific cooperation contribute to scientific innovation
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The effect of strong and weak ties on innovation in social networks has been established in the fields of technology and products, but this impact deserves more attention in the fields of knowledge and scientific innovation. To investigate the correlation between strong and weak ties and innovation in scientific collaboration, we propose a novel method for measuring tie strength on a temporal cumulative cooperative network. Based on this new method, we quantified the tie strength and innovation across 209,720 articles in the fields of quantum information and synthetic biology in the Web of Science from 2008 to 2017, and analyzed their relationships. The research results show that innovation increases as the tie strength decreases, and the growth rate of innovation becomes faster as the tie strength further decreases. Furthermore, among the 109,880 samples with tie strength below 0.3, those scientific collaboration with a common national background are more likely to generate breakthrough ideas. In summary, in knowledge creation, we reiterate the primacy of weak ties and highlight the importance of intra-regional scientific cooperation.

entries.authors: Ashkan Ebadi, Alain Auger, Yvan Gauthier
entries.title: WISDOM: An AI-powered framework for emerging research detection using weak signal analysis and advanced topic modelling
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The landscape of science and technology is characterized by its dynamic and evolving nature, constantly reshaped by discoveries, innovations, and paradigm shifts. Moreover, science is undergoing a remarkable shift towards increasing interdisciplinary collaboration, where the convergence of diverse fields fosters innovative solutions to complex problems. Detecting emerging scientific topics is paramount as it enables industries, policymakers, and innovators to adapt their strategies, investments, and regulations proactively. As the common approach for detecting emerging technologies, despite being useful, bibliometric analyses may suffer from oversimplification and/or misinterpretation of complex interdisciplinary trends. In addition, relying solely on domain experts to pinpoint emerging technologies from science and technology trends might restrict the ability to systematically analyze extensive information and introduce subjective judgments into the interpretations. To overcome these drawbacks, in this work, we present an automated artificial intelligence-enabled framework, called WISDOM, for (1) detecting emerging research themes using advanced topic modelling and weak signal analysis, and (2) generating candidate labels for identified themes to assist experts. The proposed approach can assist strategic planners and domain experts in more effectively recognizing and tracking trends related to emerging topics by swiftly processing and analyzing vast volumes of data, uncovering hidden cross-disciplinary patterns, and offering unbiased insights, thereby enhancing the efficiency and objectivity of the detection process. As the case technology, we assess WISDOM's performance in identifying emerging research as well as its trends, in the field of underwater sensing technologies using scientific papers published between 2004 and 2021.

entries.authors: Tolga Yuret
entries.title: Assessing scientific output through self-evaluation: Evidence from four social science fields
entries.primary_abstract_preview: We asked academics from the economics, political science, psychology, and sociology departments of the top 500 universities to state their top 3 publications. 2331 researchers who work in 42 countries responded to the survey. We collected the respondents’ Google Scholar (GS) and Scopus profiles to identify the publications which they did and did not select as their top 3 publications. Therefore, our study links researchers’ self-evaluated top publications with detailed bibliometric profiles, enabling a comparison between subjective assessments and bibliometric statistics. Around 30 % of respondents’ top 3 publications in political science and sociology are not indexed in Scopus, largely because many are books or non-English works. The top 3 publications demonstrate greater citation performance and are published in higher-impact journals compared to the average output. However, only 40 % of the publications identified as top 3 in self-evaluations also rank among the top 3 by citation performance. Self-evaluations offer additional insights that complement bibliometric measures, helping to address issues such as limited coverage, neglect of locally relevant research, and underrepresentation of certain academic fields.

entries.authors: Wei Cheng, Xiaomin Zheng, Dejun Zheng, Ming Li, Tianshi Cong
entries.title: A multi-dimensional indicator system for identifying highly innovative papers: a knowledge absorption, creation, and diffusion perspective
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Conventional metrics often emphasize a single aspect of academic innovation, such as citation counts, topical novelty, or disruption, and therefore fail to capture the multi-mechanism processes through which academic innovation emerges and spreads. This study develops a multi-dimensional indicator system grounded in a knowledge-evolution perspective that conceptualizes innovation across three stages: knowledge absorption, creation, and diffusion. Each stage corresponds to distinct, measurable traces in citation networks and textual semantics. Furthermore, the framework integrates citation- and content-based indicators and refines topic-novelty and knowledge-disruption measures through semantic and temporal modeling to reduce granularity and aggregation bias. Empirical validation is conducted using 1940 publications by Price Medal recipients and their cited and citing records (54,045 unique documents). Robustness is further examined through inter-indicator correlation analysis, comparison with citation impact, case validation using top-ranked innovative papers and representative works by Loet Leydesdorff, as well as a cross-field validation experiment. Results demonstrate that the proposed system effectively identifies highly innovative research and captures domain-specific patterns of knowledge generation and dissemination, offering a comprehensive and scalable approach for evaluating academic innovation.

entries.authors: Giovanni Abramo, Ciriaco Andrea D’Angelo
entries.title: Sex bias in peer review and citation practices: Implications for research evaluation
entries.primary_abstract_preview: This study examines the effectiveness of peer review versus bibliometric analysis in reducing sex bias in research evaluations. Drawing on theoretical insights from psychological, sociological, and rational choice frameworks, as well as empirical data from Italy’s first national research assessment exercise (VTR 2001–2003), we conduct a comprehensive comparison between peer-review scores and citation-based metrics across various scientific fields. Our findings reveal substantial and consistent evidence of gender-based disparities disadvantaging female-authored publications. Through ordered logistic regression analyses, we demonstrate that while both evaluation methods exhibit sex bias, peer review systematically penalizes women more severely than citation-based metrics. This disparity remains evident across varying citation windows, despite a long-term Matthew effect that slightly increases sex disparities over extended citation periods. We conclude that bibliometric evaluations, though not entirely free from bias, represent a relatively fairer alternative for assessing research output, holding crucial implications for institutional policy and the pursuit of academic equity.

entries.authors: Dar-Zen Chen, You-Fu Lee, Huei-Ru Dong, Chun-Chieh Wang
entries.title: Tracking vibrant assignees in technological innovation: A patent-based dual perspective of activity and persistence
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Sustained innovation is increasingly critical in dynamic technological environments, yet conventional patentometric measures often provide only static views of R&D performance. This study develops a dual-lens framework to identify “vibrant assignees”—organizations that combine high activity with persistent engagement in patenting. We operationalize these dimensions through a sliding-window–based Activity Index and Persistence Index, and further integrate them into a composite Vibrant Intensity indicator. Grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the framework captures both seizing capabilities, reflected in bursts of inventive activity, and transforming capabilities, reflected in sustained commitment over time. Applying this approach to 981 USPTO patents on solid-state electrolytes (2002–2021) across 223 assignees, we reveal divergent innovation strategies: Toyota Motor demonstrates long-term vibrancy across multiple subfields, while Samsung Electronics illustrates adaptive re-entry patterns. These findings highlight how organizational strategies differ between stable leadership and agile adaptation. Beyond the empirical case, the framework offers a transferable tool for patentometric and informetric studies, enabling policymakers, R&D managers, and scholars to better evaluate the temporal dynamics of technological leadership.

entries.authors: F. Pacheco-Torgal
entries.title: Comments on the ideological and philosophical foundations of bibliometrics by Gorraiz, J.
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Juan Gorraiz’s (2025) paper presents a metaphorical and conceptually rich examination of the ideological and philosophical foundations of bibliometrics, emphasizing their symbolic, heuristic, and interpretive roles in scholarly communication. While aligned with responsible research assessment initiatives such as DORA and the Leiden Manifesto, the paper lacks practical guidance, operational frameworks, and empirical evidence. Studies show that well-calibrated citation metrics are cost-efficient, predictive, and can complement peer review. Portuguese research assessments reveal that experts rely implicitly on metrics even when formally prohibited, highlighting tensions between normative principles and practice. Hybrid evaluation models that integrate bibliometrics with expert judgment better capture the multidimensional nature of scientific excellence, balancing efficiency, transparency, and ethical responsibility. Gorraiz’s work stimulates reflection but requires operational grounding to guide policy effectively.

entries.authors: Yi Zhao, Yongjun Zhu, Donghun Kim, Yuzhuo Wang, ... Chengzhi Zhang
entries.title: The effect of gender diversity on scientific team impact: A team roles perspective
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The influence of gender diversity on the success of scientific teams is of great interest to academia. However, prior findings remain inconsistent, and most studies operationalize diversity in aggregate terms, overlooking internal role differentiation. This limitation obscures a more nuanced understanding of how gender diversity shapes team impact. In particular, the effect of gender diversity across different team roles remains poorly understood. To this end, we define a scientific team as all coauthors of a paper and measure team impact through five-year citation counts. Using author contribution statements, we classified members into leadership and support roles. Drawing on more than 130,000 papers from PLOS journals, most of which are in biomedical-related disciplines, we employed multivariable regression to examine the association between gender diversity in these roles and team impact. Furthermore, we apply a threshold regression model to investigate how team size moderates this relationship. The results show that (1) the relationship between gender diversity and team impact follows an inverted U-shape for both leadership and support groups; (2) teams with an all-female leadership group and an all-male support group achieve higher impact than other team types. Interestingly, (3) the effect of leadership-group gender diversity is significantly negative for small teams but becomes positive and statistically insignificant in large teams. In contrast, the estimates for support-group gender diversity remain significant and positive, regardless of team size.

entries.authors: Kiyotaka Yabe, Mamoru Takata, Kenji Matsuura
entries.title: Breaking barriers in academic communication: Insights from a novel face-to-face interaction tracking app at an international conference
entries.primary_abstract_preview: International conferences play a crucial role in fostering collaborative research, which is essential for advancing scientific progress, especially as global challenges demand increased international collaboration. On-site conferences, in particular, enable face-to-face interactions that foster serendipitous encounters and in-depth information exchange, underscoring the need for thoughtful event designs that maximize such opportunities. However, real-world patterns of conference interactions remain poorly understood due to the difficulty of tracking participant behavior, potentially obscuring communication gaps associated with participants’ attributes. In this study, using a newly developed web application, we obtained a detailed visualization and quantification of the face-to-face interaction dynamics among 2,216 self-selected app users (out of 4,041 total participants) at the 27th International Congress of Entomology (ICE2024 KYOTO), revealing several communication gaps. The application offered a profile exchange function as a supportive, gamified feature for face-to-face networking, generating logs that allowed us to reconstruct a large-scale network of on-site communications. Analysis showed that country pairs sharing a common language and individuals with similar research fields were more likely to interact, while students and non-students interacted less frequently than expected under random mixing. Additionally, timestamp data identified sessions and events with particularly high interaction frequencies, illustrating how conference settings may influence communication. The log data provide a detailed view of the previously unmeasured dynamics and disparities in communication patterns during the conference. Our method, based on participants’ voluntary use of the application, offers a scalable approach to quantifying networking activities and provides valuable insights for designing more effective and inclusive conferences.

entries.authors: Xianwen Wang, Pengfei Jia, Weixi Xie
entries.title: Does open access promote interdisciplinary knowledge flow? A Quasi-Natural experiment of journal transitions to fully OA in agronomy
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Interdisciplinary knowledge diffusion is critical for addressing complex scientific and societal problems, yet rigid disciplinary boundaries often constrain citation flows across fields. Open Access (OA) has been advocated as a mechanism to improve research visibility and accessibility, but its effect on interdisciplinary citation remains insufficiently examined. This study evaluates the impact of OA on the breadth of interdisciplinary knowledge dissemination. Exploiting a quasi-natural experiment stemming from journal transitions to fully OA in the field of agronomy (2000–2024), we analyze over 57,000 articles and 1.5 million citing records using a multilayer disciplinary classification system. Employing negative binomial regressions and difference-in-differences estimations, we find that OA significantly broadens the disciplinary scope of citations at the topic, subfield, field, and domain levels. Mechanism analysis indicates that OA enhances dissemination via social media and public platforms, facilitating greater knowledge spillovers. These results emphasize OA’s institutional function in advancing both research accessibility and interdisciplinary knowledge convergence.

entries.authors: Xiaojuan Liu, Nannan Xiang, Mu-hsuan Huang
entries.title: How highly cited papers affect LIS journal impact factor? An empirical study
entries.primary_abstract_preview: The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is a predominant indicator in academic evaluation. However, its validity may be compromised by the highly skewed distribution of citations within the same journal, which can lead to misinterpretations in research assessment. In light of these concerns, this study examines journals in the field of Library and Information Science (LIS) by applying different treatments of highly cited papers to evaluate their influence on JIF values and ranking outcomes. To enhance comprehension of JIF-based evaluation results, the Citation Concentration Index (CCI) is proposed, which reflects the distribution of citation counts among the papers in a journal. The analysis reveals that highly cited papers are more prevalent in top-ranked journals and exert a substantial influence on JIF, while for certain lower-ranked journals, the citation counts are all relatively low, and their JIFs are more dominated by a very small number of papers. These findings underscore that JIF-based journal rankings should be interpreted in conjunction with the citation distribution of papers within each journal.

entries.authors: Yezhu Wang, Yundong Xie, Qing Ye, Lu Guo, Rongting Zhou
entries.title: Cover effects on social attention: Evidence from Cell Biology, Multidisciplinary Chemistry, and Applied Physics
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Social media has transformed scholarly communication by extending research visibility beyond citations to broader public engagement. This study investigates whether cover papers attract higher social attention, as measured by altmetrics. Drawing on 1.46 million papers (2012–2024) from the disciplines of Cell Biology, Multidisciplinary Chemistry, and Applied Physics, we apply coarsened exact matching and regression models to assess the effect of cover status on altmetric indicators. The results reveal that cover papers consistently receive higher Altmetric Attention Scores than comparable non-cover papers. This effect is stronger in high-impact and open access journals (particularly in Multidisciplinary Chemistry and Applied Physics), and in journals with embedded social media plugins. To better capture the immediate dissemination and public attention surrounding research, we propose the News and Social Media Attention Score (NSAS)—a composite metric aggregating mentions from news outlets, blogs, Twitter, and Facebook. These findings provide valuable insights for journal editors, researchers, and policymakers seeking to enhance the societal visibility and impact of scientific research.

entries.title: Design flaws in the Polish science quality evaluation system: A technical analysis of latent properties
entries.primary_abstract_preview:
In 2018, Poland’s science and higher education underwent reforms introducing a new scientometrics system to periodically evaluate research quality in about 300 institutions. This system primarily relies on parametric evaluations, with limited expert input. Evaluation outcomes affect institutions’ government funding, as well as their authority to grant academic degrees and offer study fields. Initially applied in 2022 for the 2017–2021 period, the system remains largely unchanged for the 2026 evaluation of 2022–2025, sustained more by political instability than by trust in its efficacy.

This paper examines the Polish science evaluation system through the lenses of statistics, decision-making, and operations research. We reveal four design flaws causing counterintuitive results, enabling institutions to boost scores by even 60% through creative reporting, discriminating based on size, permitting result manipulation by parties with conflicting interests, and deviating markedly from current decision science standards. Our theoretical insights are validated by data from the 2022 and 2026 evaluations. Recommendations for system improvements are also presented.

entries.title: Tracing scientific knowledge flow in patents: An explainable machine learning study of citation types and their temporal dynamics
entries.primary_abstract_preview: Patent references to scientific publications provide essential evidence of knowledge flow from science to technology, yet existing studies have rarely examined three citation types (front-page, in-text, and overlapping) or assessed how their knowledge characteristics change over time. Prior research also tends to focus on static comparisons at the level of a limited number of features, overlooking their combined contributions to knowledge flow. This study analyzes 581,684 scientific articles in biochemistry and molecular biology from 2011 to 2020, along with 230,431 patent-paper citation links involving these articles. We integrate the three citation types into a real-versus-virtual citation framework and apply XGBoost combined with SHAP and the Gini-Simpson index to assess feature contributions and their temporal dynamics. Results indicate that paper authority (normalized citation impact) and knowledge relevance (title similarity) are consistently the most influential drivers across all citation types. Front-page citations emphasize knowledge relevance, in-text citations highlight academic prestige, and overlapping citations combine both. From 2011 to 2020, all three types shift from relevance-driven to authority-driven citation behavior, with overlapping citations exhibiting intermediate trajectories. These findings provide new evidence on heterogeneous and evolving science-technology linkages and offer methodological guidance for evaluating knowledge flows in innovation studies.
